title: Perf Baseline Q1 2026 — Overview (Serving Runtime Benchmarking Suite)
author: Marcus Reed
body:
h1. Perf Baseline Q1 2026 — Overview

This page defines Redwood’s *Q1 2026 locked performance baseline* for the Serving Runtime. The baseline is a reproducible reference for end-to-end latency/throughput and runtime-internal behavior across a canonical set of models and representative traffic shapes.

The intent is that *every runtime release candidate* can be evaluated against this baseline, and that baseline artifacts can be re-run to investigate customer-impacting changes (latency, throughput, tail behavior).

*Executive sponsor:* Mateo Alvarez (Runtime)
*Program manager:* Talia Benson
*Baseline maintainer:* Marcus Reed

---

h2. Why this baseline exists (objectives)

1) *Release qualification:* Provide a mandatory, consistent perf gate for runtime release candidates (RCs) and high-risk runtime changes.
2) *Regression detection and triage:* Detect perf regressions early (nightly + PR-level micro checks) and provide enough instrumentation to explain deltas.
3) *Model catalog performance profiles:* Feed curated, reproducible performance profiles for top-served models under standard traffic shapes.
4) *Customer performance transparency (internal-first):* Enable consistent internal statements about perf behavior; external sharing is governed by Product approval (see PM workflow).

Non-goals:
- This is not a public benchmark leaderboard.
- This suite is not a substitute for customer-specific POCs; it is a standardized baseline for *comparisons*.
- It is not intended to cover every model in the catalog; it covers *top-served* and *strategic* models for runtime health.

---

h2. Baseline philosophy (what “locked” means)

We treat the baseline suite as a versioned product artifact.

*Locked* means:
- Workloads are defined by a versioned suite (traffic shape definitions, distributions, seeds, prompt sets, and run phases).
- Environment is pinned (runtime build metadata, CUDA/driver, container digest, kernel auto-selection determinism settings).
- Output schema is stable and comparable across runs.

The baseline is designed to answer:
- “Did we get faster/slower?”
- “Is the difference real or noise?”
- “If slower, is it scheduler, kernel selection, KV cache, telemetry, or fleet drift?”

Principles:
- *Prefer representativeness over maximal coverage.* We benchmark a small number of canonical shapes that map to common customer patterns.
- *Measure what users feel, and what engineers can act on.* We always include client-visible latencies plus runtime scheduler metrics.
- *Tail latency is a first-class metric.* We plan for explainability (queueing, batch composition, backpressure, load-shedding counters).

Reference ADRs:
- ADR-001: Baseline artifact versioning and retention
- ADR-002: Workload suite source of truth (repo ownership + change control)

---

h2. Definitions (metrics and how to interpret them)

All metrics are reported as p50/p95/p99 unless explicitly noted.

h3. Primary client-visible metrics

*TTFT (Time To First Token)*
- Definition: elapsed time from request accepted by the server to the first generated token being available to the client.
- For streaming: TTFT is measured to the *first streamed chunk that contains generated tokens* (not headers/keepalives).
- Why it matters: dominates perceived responsiveness.

*TPOT (Time Per Output Token)*
- Definition: average time per generated output token during decode (excluding TTFT).
- Reported as distribution across requests; also includes mean as a quick sanity check.
- Why it matters: sustained generation speed; affects long responses.

*E2E Latency (Total)*
- Definition: request completion time (server-accept → last token emitted / response complete).
- For streaming: this includes the full stream duration.

*Throughput*
- Definition: output tokens/sec aggregated at the benchmark driver (and validated against server-side token counters).
- Note: throughput must be considered alongside concurrency and error rate.

*Error rate*
- Definition: fraction of requests failing due to non-expected errors (timeouts, overload rejection beyond the workload spec, internal errors).
- Baseline runs are only valid if error rate is within the traffic shape’s allowed envelope.

h3. Runtime/internal explainability metrics (required)

These are used to explain p95/p99 movement.
- Scheduler queue wait time (histograms)
- Batch size and batch composition (prefill vs decode mix)
- Prefill utilization vs decode utilization
- Backpressure / load-shedding counters
- Token counters (input/output tokens) by phase
- KV cache hit/miss annotations (where applicable for cache scenarios)

See: “Scheduler metrics required for baselines” for the authoritative list and expected units.

---

h2. Canonical traffic-shape taxonomy (what we run)

Traffic shapes are defined in the *Representative Traffic Shapes Taxonomy* page and implemented in the benchmark harness.

Each traffic shape specifies:
- Prompt length distribution (tokens)
- Output length distribution (tokens)
- Streaming vs non-streaming
- Concurrency regime (steady, ramp, burst)
- Cache scenario (cold, warm, mixed hit rate)
- Allowed overload behavior (e.g., controlled 429s for load-shedding shapes)

At a high level, Q1 2026 baseline includes:
- *Chat steady-state (streaming)*: median prompts, moderate outputs, stable concurrency
- *Chat bursty (streaming)*: concurrency spikes + scheduler fairness pressure
- *Long-context (streaming)*: high prefill cost, sensitive to kernel selection and KV memory pressure
- *Non-streaming batch-friendly generation*: tests batching heuristics under mixed prompt lengths
- *Cache warm/hit scenarios*: validates prefix/KV caching behavior and avoids regressions in cache accounting

---

h2. Model / hardware / region matrix (Q1 2026)

This matrix lists *baseline-critical* models for Q1 2026 and where we run them. The detailed model variants, context length caps, and quantization profiles are tracked in the model matrix sheet; this page is the published summary.

Notes:
- Hardware SKUs are pinned per run; we do not mix SKUs within a single baseline comparison.
- Regions are chosen to cover representative fleet diversity without exploding variance and cost.

h3. Baseline matrix summary

|| Model family (baseline name) || Typical use || Context band || Quantization profile(s) || Hardware SKUs || Regions || Run priority ||
| Redwood-Chat-L (open chat) | Streaming chat / agentic | 8k + 32k long-context subset | FP16 + INT8 (where supported) | H100-80GB, A100-80GB | us-east-1, eu-west-1 | P0 |
| Redwood-Chat-M (cost-optimized chat) | High-volume chat | 8k | FP16 + INT8 | L40S, A100-80GB | us-east-1, us-west-2 | P0 |
| Redwood-Instruct-L (non-stream gen) | Tool output / summaries | 8k | FP16 | H100-80GB | us-east-1 | P1 |
| Redwood-LongCtx-L (long-context) | Long-doc Q&A / codebase chat | 32k–128k | FP16 (INT8 experimental only; excluded from gating unless flagged) | H100-80GB | us-east-1, eu-west-1 | P0 |
| Redwood-Embed-L (embeddings) | Embeddings | n/a | FP16 | A100-80GB, L40S | us-east-1 | P1 |
| Redwood-Rerank-M (rerank) | Reranking | n/a | FP16 | L40S | us-east-1 | P2 |

Important: The *gating set* (required for runtime RC qualification) is a subset of the above (see “How to consume” below).

---

h2. Measurement methodology (what makes runs comparable)

The authoritative methodology lives in: *Benchmark Methodology and Variance Budget*.

This page summarizes the key rules that determine whether a run is valid and comparable:

h3. Run phases
1) *Environment verification:* driver/CUDA/container digest, runtime build metadata stamp, region/SKU confirmation, clock sanity.
2) *Warmup:* run traffic shape warmup to stabilize caches and runtime steady-state (as specified per shape).
3) *Measurement trials:* fixed number of trials per shape with pinned seeds.
4) *Cooldown / reset:* where required to avoid cross-shape contamination.

h3. Reporting
- Always report: TTFT, TPOT, E2E latency, throughput, error rate.
- Always report: p50/p95/p99 and sample counts.
- Always record: commit SHA, build ID, container digest, CUDA/driver versions, benchmark runner version, and workload suite version.

h3. Variance budgets
- Each traffic shape has an acceptable variance envelope. If a delta is within the variance budget, it is treated as *noise* unless corroborated.
- Cross-region comparisons are *not* used to assert regressions. Regressions are evaluated within the same region/SKU lane unless explicitly approved.

---

h2. How teams should consume the baseline

h3. 1) Runtime release qualification (required)
Owner: Connor O’Brien (Release Engineering)

A runtime release candidate is not considered “qualified” until it has:
- A passing baseline run for the *gating set* on the *primary lane* (us-east-1 + H100-80GB) for P0 traffic shapes.
- No regressions beyond policy thresholds, or an approved exception with sign-off.

Gating set (Q1 2026):
- Redwood-Chat-L: chat steady-state (streaming), chat bursty (streaming)
- Redwood-LongCtx-L: long-context streaming

When a release is blocked:
- File a regression ticket under the parent initiative and link the run artifacts.
- Use the tail latency triage playbook to determine whether it’s kernels, scheduler, KV cache, telemetry, or fleet drift.

h3. 2) PR-level checks (early warning; not a substitute for the baseline)
Owner: Sahana Iyer (CI/nightly perf automation)

We run a “perf smoke” job on key microbenchmarks for runtime PRs.
- Purpose: catch obvious regressions quickly.
- Scope: smaller and cheaper than baseline; higher noise.
- Policy: warn-only initially; blocking behavior follows the rollout plan and the Perf Regression Policy.

h3. 3) Nightly baseline drift detection
Owner: Sean Gallagher (SRE)

Nightly jobs run the baseline suite against mainline to detect drift.
- Alerts are configured as *warn-only* unless the regression exceeds “severe” thresholds.
- When an alert fires, operators must first check environment drift (driver/CUDA mismatch, SKU mix) before escalating.

h3. 4) Model catalog performance profiles
Owner: Quentin Harris (Model catalog perf profiles)

Baseline results are used to populate internal performance profiles.
- Profiles are tagged with workload suite version and environment lane.
- External sharing requires Product approval (Henry Cho / Paula Mendes), and must follow confidentiality constraints.

---

h2. Dashboards, artifacts, and where results live

h3. Dashboards (Grafana + Console)
See: *Perf Baseline Dashboards Spec*

Required dashboard dimensions:
- model
- traffic shape
- region
- hardware SKU
- runtime commit SHA / build ID

Standard drilldowns:
- compare vs last baseline tag
- compare vs last 7 days median
- overlay queue wait and batch composition vs TTFT/TPOT p99

h3. Artifacts (what is stored)
For every baseline run we store:
- Summary metrics (p50/p95/p99 TTFT/TPOT/E2E, throughput, error rate)
- Raw histograms (where supported) and sample counts
- Workload suite version and config bundle checksum
- Prompt set identifiers (no raw sensitive prompts; see confidentiality rules)
- Runtime build metadata, container digest, CUDA/driver versions
- Scheduler metrics snapshot required for explainability

Retention:
- Baseline tags: retained indefinitely for Q1 2026
- Nightly runs: retained per ADR-001 policy

---

h2. Confidentiality and data handling

This baseline suite is built to avoid storing customer-sensitive prompt content.

Rules:
- No raw customer prompts are stored in baseline artifacts.
- Representative workloads derived from production signals must be *aggregated/sanitized* and approved by Applied ML perf/evals + Security if needed.
- Any plan to share metrics externally must follow the Product approval workflow and avoid disclosing restricted fleet or customer information.

If you think a workload shape might leak sensitive information, stop and escalate to the program manager + Security & Compliance.

---

h2. Change control (how this page and the baseline evolves)

- The workload suite is the source of truth; this page summarizes the current baseline and should be updated when baseline tags change.
- Any change that affects comparability (definitions, shapes, environment pinning) requires:
  1) ADR or documented rationale
  2) reviewer sign-off (Runtime + SRE + Methodology)
  3) new baseline tag

See:
- Perf Regression Policy (company standard)
- ADR-001 / ADR-002
